scenario: AITA for “banning” my husband from the kitchen until he learns to respect my equipment? | I love to cook, I’ve been cooking since I was a little kid. I have some good cooking equipment that reflects that fact. My husband decided that he was going to start cooking as well, which I was all for. But he started cooking in the kitchen and damaging my equipment. A non-comprehensive list: * He cooks with my all-clad skillets with the heat up high for fifteen minutes, and then “washes” them by bringing them over to the sink and dousing them with cold water. He says he “likes the sizzle.” At least one of the skillets is warping a bit, it won’t sit straight on the stove anymore and doesn’t cook evenly. * He uses my chef’s knife to scrape crud off the counter. I told him to use my razor blade scraper to do it, he said “well, that would be overkill.” * I have a small toaster oven that acts as a mini-oven, I absolutely love. He butters toast BEFORE putting it in the oven. The fat drips onto the element. He did this so much that I’ve already had to have the element replaced once. He continues to do it and says “we can just replace it again.” * He cooked a tomato sauce in my seasoned cast iron skillet and then ran it through the dishwasher. * He leaves lemon juice, tomato, vinegar spills all over the granite countertops. When I tell him to clean up immediately, he laughs and says, “it’s granite, it’s indestructible!” This all annoyed me so much. I’m annoyed just typing it. Finally I told him that unless he starts actually respecting my equipment, I’m going to put it all under lock and key. He said, “what, you’re banishing me from the kitchen? From my own house?” I said “yes, you’re ruining all of my things.” He implied that it all belonged to him since he “bought it,” but I am fully aware that I had all of this stuff and bought all of this stuff before we got married. AITA? All I want is for him to respect my things. He knows that I hate when he does this stuff but he shouts and yells and calls me over critical every time I try to explain it to him. I’m at my wit’s end.

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

I’m at my wit’s end.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **1** (a fair and reasonable response in the context of the situation). ### **Why?** You’re absolutely within your rights to set boundaries around your property—especially when it’s being damaged or disrespected. Your kitchen equipment is yours (or jointly owned, but you clearly put significant effort into acquiring and maintaining it), and your husband’s actions are causing avoidable wear and tear. His dismissive attitude ("it’s granite, it’s indestructible") and refusal to take responsibility for his mistakes are unreasonable. ### **Key Points Supporting Your Side:** 1. **Your Property, Your Rules** – If you bought the equipment and maintain it, you have every right to decide how it’s used. Even if it’s a shared home, you’re not obligated to tolerate abuse of your belongings. 2. **His Actions Are Negligent** – Running skillets under cold water, using a knife as a scraper, buttering toast before baking, and running cast iron through the dishwasher are all **proven ways to damage cookware**. His excuses ("I like the sizzle," "it’s granite") are lazy and dismissive. 3. **He’s Not Trying to Fix It** – You’ve already had to replace a toaster oven element once because of his habits, and he’s still doing it. That’s not a one-time mistake—it’s a pattern of disrespect. 4. **His Tone Is Unreasonable** – Yelling and calling you "overcritical" when you’re explaining basic care is gaslighting. If he can’t respect your boundaries, he’s the one being unreasonable. ### **Where He Might Have a Weak Point (But Not Enough to Override Your Rights):** - **He may have contributed financially** to the home/kitchen, but that doesn’t mean he owns your specific items. If you bought them before marriage, they’re yours (unless you have a prenuptial agreement stating otherwise). - **He’s being childish**—his reaction ("banishing me from my own house?") is dramatic and unfair. If he can’t respect your things, he can still cook (e.g., in a separate pan or with his own gear). ### **What You Could Do Next:** - **Lock it up temporarily** (if that’s what it takes to stop the damage). - **Buy cheap replacement pans** for him to use until he learns proper care. - **Set a clear consequence** (e.g., "If this continues, I’m replacing all damaged items out of my own pocket"). - **Document the damage** (take photos) in case he tries to claim it was "always like this." ### **Final Verdict:** You’re **not** being unreasonable. His behavior is careless, dismissive, and damaging. If he can’t respect your things, he should either: - **Learn proper care** (and stop making excuses), or - **Use his own gear** (if he’s unwilling to respect yours). Either way, **you’re not obligated to tolerate abuse of your property**. If he can’t handle that, that’s his problem—not yours.
